name: Law of Proximity
description: Elements placed near one another are more likely to be perceived as belonging together. Spacing itself communicates structure before labels or borders do.
design_relevance_note: Directly informs grouping of form fields, card content, navigation items, tables, settings sections, and dashboard clusters; whitespace can create or break perceived relationships without adding extra chrome.
prevalence_note: One of the basic Gestalt laws taught in visual-design, layout, and information-architecture fundamentals; spacing/grouping is core day-to-day design-crit vocabulary.

findings.description: Reviewing a century of Gestalt and modern vision-science work, Wagemans et al. conclude that classical grouping principles such as proximity and similarity — along with newer principles such as uniform connectedness — remain core, empirically studied mechanisms of perceptual organization, with documented roles in contour integration and figure-ground organization.
findings.source_title: A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception: I. Perceptual grouping and figure-ground organization.

applications.title: Amazon's product-listing grid uses proximity to group related items
applications.description: Amazon's product-listing pages group similar or related products together using narrow whitespace between items within a group and wider gaps between groups, applying the Gestalt Law of Proximity so users can visually parse which products belong together without needing to read every label.
applications.ethical_note: A straightforward information-organization aid -- grouping related products so users can parse a page faster -- with no persuasion or manipulation dimension; it helps users find what they're looking for rather than steering them toward a particular choice.

applications.title: Wellington City Council's site separates Search from navigation using whitespace, responsively
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's article on the proximity principle describes how the Wellington City Council website's header places its Search function on the same line as the main navigation, but uses extra whitespace to separate Search from the navigation items -- signaling, via proximity alone, that Search is a distinct type of functionality even though it shares the same font treatment as the navigation links. On smaller screens where that whitespace can't be maintained, the design instead moves Search up and groups it with other utility-menu items, preserving the same proximity-based grouping logic responsively rather than letting Search visually collapse into the main navigation.
applications.ethical_note: A structural clarity technique, applied responsively, that helps users tell Search apart from navigation at any screen size; no persuasive or manipulative dimension.
